alalal-c48048-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 19: whether the divine essence alone is wholly non-local, uncircumscribable and immobile.

alalal-c48048-d1e113.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's statement that the divine essence alone is wholly non-local and uncircumscribable.

alalal-c48048-d1e127.summary: Objection: Augustine says to Orosius that God moves himself without place and time.

alalal-c48048-d1e137.summary: Objection: Dionysius in the Divine Names speaks of processions befitting the good, by which God moves and proceeds into all that is according to each one's analogy for participating his goodness.

alalal-c48048-d1e155.summary: Objection: Habakkuk 3:13 says God went forth for the salvation of his people, and Scripture often speaks of God going forth and walking among the saints; other objections appear in the earlier discussion of immutability.

alalal-c48048-d1e173.summary: Solution with Boethius: God, remaining stable, gives motion to all. Wherever Scripture says God moves, proceeds or walks, it refers to his effects, making the saints advance in him or creatures progress, or to an assumed creature.
claims: God is immobile; scriptural ascriptions of motion to him refer to his effects or to an assumed creature.

alalal-c48048.summary: Article 19 defends Lombard's claim that the divine essence alone is wholly non-local, uncircumscribable and immobile, against Augustine's talk of God moving himself, Dionysius' processions of the good into all things, and scriptural language of God going forth and walking. Following Boethius, Albert holds that God, remaining stable, moves all things. Ascriptions of motion to God refer either to his effects, such as the saints' progress in him, or to an assumed creature.
claims: The divine essence alone is non-local, uncircumscribable and immobile.
Scriptural and patristic language of divine motion refers to God's effects or to an assumed creature.
